entries.title: Gabriela Jaquez provides a refresher on why the Sky drafted her at No. 5
entries.summary: <p>With six UCLA players drafted into the WNBA this season, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> rookie <b>Gabriela Jaquez</b> rarely goes long without facing an old teammate. Last week, it was <b>Lauren Betts</b> and <b>Angela Dugalic</b> of the Mystics.</p><p>On Tuesday, it was her good friend <b>Kiki Rice</b>. Drafted by the Tempo one spot behind Jaquez at No. 6, Rice has had an impressive rookie season, running the offense and averaging 13.4 points.</p><p>But Jaquez won the matchup Tuesday night, scoring 18 points in the Sky’s 97-85 win over the Tempo.</p><p>“You can tell who she is every single time she steps on the floor,” Rice said of Jaquez. “She’s gonna play hard, she’s gonna find ways to score.</p><p>“She’s the kind of player you want on your team.”</p><p>Jaquez fell out of the Sky rotation midway through the season and averaged just seven points, so Rice owns the better stat line for the year.</p><p>But now that Jaquez is back in a starting role, she’s showed more of why the Sky bet on her, averaging 14 points in the last three games.</p><p><b>First timers</b></p><p>The Sky’s late-season focus on their younger players has given two recent additions a chance to play.</p><p>Development player <b>Morgan Maly</b> scored the first basket of her WNBA career against the Dream, then followed it with eight points and four rebounds against the Tempo.</p><p>“I’m just trying to come in here and learn and try to fit the system and what they want to do,” she told the Sun-Times before the game.</p><p><b>Kate Martin</b>, another development player whom the Sky picked up after the Sparks released her, also got her first minutes. The Edwardsville, Illinois native hit her first three in a Sky uniform and had her mom and her old trainer in the stands to watch her do it.</p>
entries.author: Alissa Hirsh

entries.title: CPD searching for man who sexually assaulted woman on Blue Line train
entries.summary: <p>Chicago police are looking for a man wanted for allegedly sexually assaulting a woman on the Blue Line Monday evening.</p><p>The woman was on a train near the 4000 block of W Irving Park Road at 6:38 p.m. when the reported attacker sat behind her and assaulted her before fleeing the train, police said.</p><p>Police ask anyone with information contact Public Transportation Unit detectives at 312-745-4447.</p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Potential nor’easter threatens Cubs’ final regular-season series in Boston with possible playoff implications
entries.summary: <p>The only thing the Cubs might be paying closer attention to than the scoreboard this week is the forecast.</p><p>Where’s <b>Tom Skilling</b> when you need him?</p><p>A nor’easter – a powerful storm with heavy rains and strong winds, for us Midwesterners not familiar with the specifics of East Coast weather – could make its way to Boston this weekend, threatening the Cubs’ final series of the regular season against the Red Sox at Fenway Park.</p><p>“It sounds like lovely weather ahead,” team president <b>Jed Hoyer</b> joked Tuesday.</p><p>Even before the beginning of their penultimate series of the campaign, against the Marlins at Wrigley Field, what might happen this weekend was a prominent topic of conversation.</p><p>Not only are the playoffs set to begin next Tuesday, giving little time to squeeze in any makeup games, but the games could be all-important in ironing out the bunched-up NL wild-card standings.</p><p>The Cubs started Tuesday tied with the Padres for the No. 1 wild-card spot, both teams only a game ahead of the Phillies. Should they stay tightly packed until the weekend, those contests will place the three teams, as well as determine who gets home-field advantage in the opening round.</p><p>Right now, there are still four different possibilities for where the Cubs could play a best-of-three series: Chicago, Philadelphia, San Diego and Atlanta.</p><p>So getting those games played – rather than bumping any of them to the Monday in between the end of the regular season and the start of the postseason – would obviously be preferred. Otherwise, the Cubs could end up playing Monday on the East Coast and, though it’s just one of many possibilities, flying to the West Coast for a Tuesday game against the Padres.</p><p>Hoyer didn’t offer any comments on suggestions that game times get moved or that the games themselves get moved to another city altogether.</p><p>But the Red Sox are also bound for the wild-card round and wouldn’t want to deal with those headaches, either.</p><p>“We’ve been in touch with the Red Sox and MLB,” Hoyer said. “Nothing’s decided yet, but certainly, we’re aware it’s a really bad forecast. Those things change a lot, so we’ll monitor the weather. But certainly, it’s something that’s on everyone’s radar.</p><p>“Exactly which days are in jeopardy and those things are still moving around, so we want to let that sort itself out a little bit. But it’s good that the two sides have been having discussions since yesterday.</p><p>“Playing Monday is obviously not a positive for anyone. But we’re trying to work through the different scenarios. Everyone’s aware of it. It’s [only] Tuesday.”</p><p><b>Shota in Game 1?</b></p><p>Will the Cubs tab lefty <b>Shota Imanaga</b> as their Game 1 playoff starter?</p><p>There’s a lot to figure out before then, but the southpaw bolstered his case Tuesday, holding the Marlins to a single run and striking out seven in five innings of work.</p><p>After struggling in September last season, Imanaga has been strong in the final month this year, with a 1.96 ERA in his last four starts.</p><p><b>Man of Steele</b></p><p>Lefty <b>Justin Steele</b> could find himself, finally, back on a big league mound before the end of the week.</p><p>“The plan is for him to be an option [to pitch] this weekend, possibly,” manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> said. “We’ll see what this weekend has in store for us and what this weekend gives us and make a decision.</p><p>“He pitched really well his last outing. And most importantly, that’s a good feeling for him, to have success and feel like, ‘I threw the ball well,’ as you work through this process of working back. That’s a great sign.”</p>
entries.author: Vinnie Duber

entries.title: Donda West Way: A South Shore street is renamed for a Chicago 'village mom'
entries.summary: <p>A group of Chicago-bred hip-hop legends gathered for a South Shore reunion, and for a moment, they transported to their teenage years — making music in the living room of their chosen mom, Donda West.</p><p>“This is not just a story about Donda West's son,” said Chicago Public Schools Board member and rapper Che “Rhymefest” Smith. “This is really a story about a woman who raised a community of boys.”</p><p>West was known for being the mother of hip-hop artist Ye, formerly known as Kanye West. To many Chicagoans, she was also an English professor, a former Chicago State University department chairperson, a businesswoman, a Fulbright scholar — and as Smith would call it, a “village mom.”</p><p>The two-story blue house on the city’s South Side was both the Wests’ home and where Ye’s music career was launched alongside his childhood friends. Now signs on 78th Street between South Shore Drive and Coles Avenue, at two nearby intersections, bear Donda West’s name.</p><p>“I love my biological mama, and I'm so proud to have a village mom like Dr. Donda West,” Smith said, with the crowd erupting in cheers.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" entries.title: Chase Meidroth 'brings fire' to surprising White Sox team
entries.summary: <p>KANSAS CITY, Mo. – Once the third piece of the four-player package the Boston Red Sox sent over for Garrett Crochet in December 2024, Chase Meidroth has blossomed into <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/21/cubs-white-sox-chicago-pete-crow-armstrong-pca-alex-bregman-munetaka-murakami-will-venable-mlb" target="_blank" ><u>the best second baseman in Chicago</u></a>.</p><p>If wins above replacement (WAR) can be trusted, Meidroth is the most valuable everyday man at the position in the American League, even before he drove in five runs in the first three innings Tuesday night at Kauffman Stadium.</p><p>Meidroth isn’t one to sing his own praises, but plenty will do it for him.</p><p>“He leaves it all out there,” said Kyle Teel, the White Sox headliner of that same trade. “He’s always going to bring everything he’s got, every single time.”</p><p>“He's a guy who brings fire,” said double play partner Colson Montgomery. “He does a lot of things that a lot of us can't do, and he plays the crap out of second base.”</p><p>Montgomery is referencing how on an offense built on power but also running the fifth-highest strikeout in the sport, Meidroth is a peskier, contact-oriented hitter who provides a frustrating change of pace to opposing pitchers. That said, much of Meidroth’s breakout is summed up by the diminutive infielder unlocking the power to drive his 16th home run of the season–easily a professional single-season high–an estimated 410 feet on Tuesday night.</p><p>Meidroth is often cited as a beneficiary of the<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/09/white-sox-hitting-director-ryan-fuller-talks-offensive-improvement-and-the-development-that-remains-colson-montgomery-munetaka-murakami-miguel-vargas-chase-meidroth" target="_blank" ><u> White Sox’ emphasis on bat speed training</u></a>, though his numbers don’t reflect a huge jump, and the occasional power strokes he allows himself are buried amid a host of shorter, slower cuts, dictated by the game situation. He’s not one to get into the weeds about his swing mechanics, but his coaches are happy to talk him up instead.</p><p>“There's a few things you could point to, but it's also knowing before two strikes, what's he using?” said hitting director Ryan Fuller. “‘When can he take his best swing over the middle of the plate, rather than the contact-oriented one he does with two strikes. It’s him understanding the game better, game-planning, the way you train, picking his spots when he’s in the box of being able to let it go a little bit.”</p><p>Nine of Meidroth’s home runs have come in 58 games since the All-Star break, and he entered Tuesday slugging .440 in the second half, despite playing much of it with a sore left wrist that has often required a brace or wrap. You can imagine how much he has to offer on that subject.</p><p>“It feels good,” Meidroth said of his wrist after a two-homer game in St. Louis earlier this month.</p><p>“He's been playing through some things a little bit, and I think that's kind of affected his offensive numbers,” Randal Grichuk told the Sun-Times. “Not necessarily here, but you play with some guys that they take the day, they want the day off. That's not him at all.”</p><p>With his all-business approach to interviews and the field, Meidroth cuts an amusing contrast to the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/18/sox-pitcher-mike-vasil-throws-for-first-time-since-tommy-john-surgery" target="_blank" ><u>bubbly persona of his in-season roommate Mike Vasil</u></a>. The rehabbing right-hander acknowledges the outward difference in personalities, but thinks there’s a lot missed behind the scenes.</p><p>“It's his ability to actually listen and learn, and ability to also admit when he doesn't feel right or is struggling, or knows he needs extra help,” Vasil said. “It kind of reflects on other guys too. Because he's constantly having conversations–whether it's with [third base coach Justin Jirschele] about defense, whether it's [Derek Shomon] about hitting, day-in and day-out–making adjustments to get better.”</p><p>As recently as last year, the White Sox internally suspected Meidroth would settle into a utility role by the time they reached contention. If the Red Sox thought differently, they wouldn’t have traded Meidroth after a dominant 2024 season in Triple-A.</p><p>But like this White Sox team he powers, Meidroth has shown that projections can only tell you so much.</p><p>“He’s still evolving,” said general manager Chris Getz. “We are here to guide him.”</p>
entries.author: James Fegan

entries.title: Facing division leaders, Royals eyeing 'spoiler role' in final week
entries.summary: <p>KANSAS CITY, Mo. — After winning seasons the past two years, the Royals enter a season-ending six-game homestand at 67-89 and as one of the bigger disappointments in the league.</p><p>Simultaneously, the road to the American League Central title runs through Kauffman Stadium.</p><p>Following three games against the second-place White Sox, the Royals will end their season this weekend by hosting the division-leading Guardians for another three-game set.</p><p>“We want to ruin somebody's season,” Royals catcher <b>Carter Jensen</b> told the Sun-Times. “We want to spoil it for somebody else. We’re obviously not going to be in the playoffs, but we want to be there. So if we can fill that spoiler role, I think it’s fun and we can show we’re not done fighting.”</p><p>Beset by pitching injuries that have seen both their opening day starter (<b>Cole Ragans</b>) and closer (<b>Carlos Estevez</b>) lost for the season, the Royals entered Tuesday losers of seven of their last eight. But with the emergence of young hitters like Jensen (.847 OPS since the All-Star break) and Jac Caglianone, Kansas City has an offense that’s allowed them to compile a 29-30 second-half record up to the final week.</p><p>With the Guardians entering Tuesday with a one-game lead and the Sox holding the season-series tiebreaker, the Royals can obviously affect the AL Central race, but also size up where they stand against the division’s best entering the offseason.</p><p>“Losing those pitchers, a few starting pitchers and bullpen pieces, it's been kind of a revolving door,” Jensen said. “We've done a great job this second half of not caring who all is here. We're just going to do the best with what we have.”</p><p>For their part, the Sox seem to understand that ending their season against two last-place teams does not equate to a cakewalk.</p><p>“We are so close to making a huge difference, not just for us but for the history of the organization,” said <b>Miguel Vargas</b>. “Accomplishing what we want is going to be hard. It’s not going to be easy.”</p><h3><b>Vargas is AL Player of the Week </b></h3><p>Vargas was named American League Player of the Week on Monday, after hitting .348/.500/.783 with three home runs from Sept. 14-20. It’s Vargas’ second time winning the award, with the first coming in May last year.</p><p>The timing makes the second time around sweeter.</p><p>“We treat this as a playoff game,” Vargas said. “Whatever we did in the past five months wouldn’t mean anything if we don’t make it.”</p><p>The Sox roster largely hasn’t been through a playoff chase before, but Vargas looks like he has the ability to raise his game.</p><p>“We’ve seen him increase his attention to detail,” said manager Will Venable. “He’s absolutely locked in right now. And I think it’s a response to where we’re at.”</p><h3><b>Peters at the ready</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Four days after a scary collision with a Rate Field outfield fence post, All-Star outfielder <b>Tristan Peters</b> is at “full availability,” though he was out of Tuesday’s starting lineup against a left-handed opposing starter.</p><p>“To give his body up to try and make a play like that speaks a lot to the kind of player he is, and being able to recover from that so quickly has been awesome," Venable said.</p><p>In Peters’ stead, <b>Brenton Doyle</b> homered in his first at-bat against southpaw Daniel Lynch IV on Tuesday.</p>
